title: Data, maps and decisions
text: I’m Eriola, a Government Operational Researcher and geospatial analyst. I’ve worked with quantitative, geospatial and statistical methods for more than 15 years, in government, academia and the private sector. Here I share my projects and write about making messy data clear, explaining uncertainty, and how AI is changing the way I work with spatial data.

title: Last orders? Drawing the UK with its pubs
text:
Can you draw the UK using only pubs? I wanted to find out.
I downloaded the Food Standards Agency food hygiene register, which lists every place that serves food or drink. I picked out all the pubs and bars, 38,022 of them, and visualised them as dots. I didn’t add any coastline, roads or towns, just the pubs, and you can still recognise the whole country.

title: Last orders? Drawing the UK with its pubs
text:
Did COVID close the pubs?
Then I wondered if COVID had an impact. I looked at the ONS data, which counts pubs and bars with staff, and found out that the big drop happened ten years earlier. The UK lost more than 9,000 pubs between 2008 and 2013, and 1,260 between 2019 and 2024. When I split them by size, it was mostly the small pubs that closed (down 44%), while the big ones actually grew.



UK pubs and bars, 2001 to 2024.

title: Last orders? Drawing the UK with its pubs
text:
The fun part
The fun part was going through the pub names. There are 361 Red Lions, and there are more animals than royals in pub names. I also looked for the streets with the most pubs (Swansea’s Wind Street has 13 bars in 186 metres) and the place furthest from a pub, which in England is 15.7 km away, in Kielder Forest.
You can also check how pubby your postcode is. Mine is “pub crawl territory”.

title: Can you draw Greece with tavernas?
text:
After drawing the UK with its pubs, I wanted to try the same with Greece. The closest thing to a pub is probably the kafeneio, but for a map I thought tavernas, kafeneia and ouzeri together would work best.
It turned out to be much harder than I expected.

title: Can you draw Greece with tavernas?
text:
Finding the data
For the UK I downloaded one register from one website, and every pub had a name, an address and coordinates. Greece doesn’t have anything like it. The food authority and the health ministry only publish summary tables of their inspections. On data.gov.gr I found only a handful of municipalities, out of 332, that publish their list of licensed shops, and some of those are PDFs or stop in 2018.
So I used OpenStreetMap. Even that wasn’t easy: the servers refused my downloads, so I had to download it by hand in the browser, and it crashed my computer. In the end I had 33,951 restaurants, cafés and bars, and I sorted them into tavernas, kafeneia and ouzeri using their names and tags.



Tavernas, ouzeri and kafeneia in OpenStreetMap.

title: Can you draw Greece with tavernas?
section: A map of tavernas, or of tourists?
text:
A map of tavernas, or of tourists?
The islands and the coast light up, and much of the north is dark. Then I compared the map with ELSTAT’s official counts of restaurants, bars and cafés, and found out that OpenStreetMap has only 46% of them. On Crete and the islands it has more than 80%, but in Pella, Xanthi and Imathia only about one in ten. So the map shows where tourists go as much as where the tavernas are.



How much of each area’s businesses are on OpenStreetMap.

title: Can you draw Greece with tavernas?
text:
The crisis and the names
ELSTAT’s numbers show about 15% fewer bars, cafés and restaurants since 2011, but twice as many people working in bars and cafés. It’s the same as the UK pubs: fewer places, but bigger ones. Attica gained bars and cafés from 2016 to 2023, while the north lost about a quarter.
The fun part was the names again. Greece doesn’t have a Red Lion. The most common name is Panorama, with only 38, followed by Akrogiali (the seashore), Nikos and, of course, Zorbas.

title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
text:
Back in 2019, during my MSc in Geoinformatics, I made a set of maps of Andros. I collected the base data from free online sources, created the digital terrain models myself and designed two printed maps at 1:150,000, one with contours and one with hypsometric tints and hillshading. I also made a web version, served through GeoServer with OpenLayers on top.
It worked well for the course. But it needed a map server running all the time, a styling file for every layer and someone to look after it. That’s not something a small island can realistically keep going.

title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
text:
What was missing
Before starting, I had a look at what’s already out there. The Municipality of Andros publishes its maps as static images. The best interactive maps of the island come from others: Andros Routes, a non-profit, looks after the trail network, and there are hiking maps you can buy. What I couldn’t find was a simple, free map of the whole island that also gives coordinates in the Greek Grid (ΕΓΣΑ87), the system local engineers work with.

title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
text:
The map
The new version is one web page, with no server behind it:

Relief first. The 13 m terrain model and the hillshade are blended into one relief image, so you can read the shape of the island straight away.
Names that suit the zoom. The generalised 1:150,000 settlements from 2019 decide which village names you see when you zoom out, so that work is still being used.
Click anywhere to get the elevation and the coordinates in both WGS84 and ΕΓΣΑ87.
Draw a route to get its length, ascent, descent and an elevation profile.
Greek and English, with a search that doesn’t mind accents, and its own symbol for every kind of feature.
OpenStreetMap layers you can switch on for everyday use: health centres, pharmacies, police and fire stations, municipal offices, fuel, bus stops, springs, viewpoints and the waymarked trails. Each trail opens its own elevation profile.




Elevation profile from Chora across the island’s central ridge

title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
text:
How I built it
I rebuilt it in Python, coding with Claude: GeoPandas for the vector layers, rasterio for the terrain and Leaflet for the map.

title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
text:
What’s next
I’d like to explore how a map like this could be useful in a council setting, for example for the Municipality of Andros, where a single file can sit inside their existing website with one line of code.
Map: etymo.co.uk/AndrosWebMap

title: Projects
text:
Planning and geospatial tools


Article 4 and constraints checker, Kingston

Web tool · JavaScript, Leaflet, Planning Data API, proj4

I built this to help with Local Land Charges searches at the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames. You can check one property by address, postcode or grid reference, or upload a CSV to check hundreds at once. Each location is checked through the government’s Planning Data service for Article 4 directions, conservation areas, listed buildings, tree preservation, green belt, flood zones and SSSIs. Anything within 10, 25 or 50 m of a boundary is flagged as borderline. Article 4 results are also checked against Kingston’s own boundaries, and the tool still works offline if the service is down.

Open the checker Code



Retrofit planning checker

Web tool · JavaScript, Leaflet, Planning Data API, HM Land Registry INSPIRE

Can this home have a heat pump, solar panels or insulation without planning permission? You enter an address, postcode or grid reference anywhere in England. For each common energy improvement, the checker tells you if it’s usually permitted development, allowed with limits, needs prior approval, or needs planning permission or listed building consent, and links to the rule. It checks listed buildings, conservation areas, Article 4 directions, protected trees, flood zones and more across the whole Land Registry plot, and takes the type of home into account. There’s also a batch mode for whole retrofit programmes. If a council hasn’t published its data, the checker says “check with the council”, so it never says “allowed” when it can’t know.

Open the checker Code



Planning Data Tracker

Web tool and weekly pipeline · Python, GitHub Actions, Leaflet

While building the Kingston checker, I found 113 Article 4 areas that didn’t link to their directions. That made me realise planning tools can only answer from what councils publish, so “no tree preservation order” might really mean “we don’t know”. This tracker shows, for all 337 local planning authorities in England, which of 10 council datasets have records in their area, from Article 4 and conservation areas to brownfield land and local green spaces. It also flags data problems with Article 4 directions. It updates every week, and you can re-check any council live.

Open the tracker Code



Takeaways near schools

Web tool · JavaScript, Leaflet, FSA and DfE open data

Many councils restrict new hot-food takeaways near schools. For any council in England, this maps every open school with a zone around it (200 to 800 m, you choose), every takeaway from the food hygiene data, and which schools have the most takeaways nearby. You can choose which school phases count, check if a proposed site falls inside a zone and download the results as CSV. I’ve listed the limits too: distances are straight lines, and food hygiene categories are not the same as planning use classes.

Open the tool Code

Remote sensing


Green Change Monitor

Web tool · Sentinel-2, NDVI, Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFFs, geotiff.js

Where were trees and green space lost or gained? You pick an area and two years, and it maps where vegetation was lost or gained using free Sentinel-2 imagery. It all runs in the browser. It finds the clearest images, masks the clouds, makes a cloud-free greenness map for each year and compares them. In England, it flags changes inside conservation areas and tree preservation areas, so planning and enforcement teams know where to look first. You can download the results as GeoJSON or CSV. It shows you where to look, but it isn’t evidence on its own.

title: Do motorcyclists follow variable message signs? What 105 riders in Athens told us
text:
Athens has had variable message signs (VMS) since 2004. These are the electronic panels over the main roads, 24 of them, run by the city’s traffic management centre. They warn drivers about accidents, roadworks and demonstrations ahead. The messages are designed for car drivers, but a big part of the traffic in Athens is on two wheels. Motorcycles and scooters filter between lanes and rarely sit in the queue the sign is warning about.
So with Ioanna Spyropoulou at the National Technical University of Athens, I wanted to find out: do riders actually change their route when a variable message sign tells them there’s a problem ahead?

title: Do motorcyclists follow variable message signs? What 105 riders in Athens told us
text:
How we did it
We stopped riders across Athens and asked them to fill in a questionnaire. This wasn’t easy, because many said no. In the end we had 105 complete answers. Each rider saw a set of made-up but realistic VMS messages. We changed three things in the messages: what the incident was, how serious its impact was, and whether the sign suggested another route. For each message, riders said how likely they were to divert. Then we used probit models to see which parts of the message, and which kinds of rider, made a diversion more likely.

title: Do motorcyclists follow variable message signs? What 105 riders in Athens told us
text:
What we found

Riders like the VMS, but they don’t feel the signs are for them. Most found them useful, but 56% didn’t want more money spent on them, and 36% wanted the VMS to show travel times based on how two-wheelers actually move.
The message matters. The type of incident and how big its impact was both changed whether riders diverted. Roadworks made them most likely to change route.
A suggested route doesn’t. Car drivers and professional drivers in earlier studies were influenced by a suggested alternative route, but riders weren’t. They find their own way.
The rider matters too. Riders on bigger motorcycles were more likely to divert, probably because they can’t get through traffic as easily. Age, gender and habits such as breaking traffic rules also played a part.

title: Do motorcyclists follow variable message signs? What 105 riders in Athens told us
text:
Why it matters
Smart city tools are often designed for one kind of road user. If a city wants its information systems to work for everyone, it needs to ask each group what they need. For riders in Athens, that means information based on how they move, which is different from how cars queue.

Spyropoulou, I. and Impersimi, E. (2020). Powered-two-wheelers and smart cities: the case of variable message signs. IET Intelligent Transport Systems, 14(14), 2021–2029. doi.org/10.1049/iet-its.2019.0702

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
In 2021 I finished my master’s thesis in Geoinformatics at the National Technical University of Athens. I looked at 1,318 pedestrian collisions in the Municipality of Athens between 2008 and 2017, and my main question was: how does the shape of the city relate to where pedestrians get injured?
I found hotspots in the centre that kept coming back, around Omonia, Syggrou and Vasilissis Sofias. I also found links with bars and pubs, crossings, traffic signals and bus stops. At the end of the thesis I wrote down what I was missing: the time of day, the age of the people involved, the socio-economic context, and some idea of how busy each place was.
Five years later I wanted to ask the same questions for London, where all of that data is available.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
The data
Almost everything I needed for London is open:

Collisions: the Department for Transport’s STATS19 data. Every injury collision recorded by the police, with location, date, time, severity and the age of each casualty.
Neighbourhoods: ONS small-area boundaries, the English Indices of Deprivation 2025 and population figures.
Streets: OpenStreetMap for crossings, signals, bus stops, stations, schools, pubs and the street network.

From 2021 to 2025 there were 22,108 pedestrian casualties in Greater London. 5,926 of them were killed or seriously injured, and between 36 and 61 people died each year.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
section: Lesson one: what you divide by changes the story
text:
Lesson one: what you divide by changes the story
When I ranked the boroughs by fatal and serious casualties per 100,000 residents, the City of London came out at 167.6 a year. That’s nearly four times Westminster (43.0), which came second. At first sight it looks like the most dangerous place to walk in London.
But only a few thousand people live in the City, and hundreds of thousands work there or pass through every weekday. So dividing by residents doesn’t really measure the risk of walking there. When I ranked the boroughs per kilometre of road instead, the order changed a lot.



The same data gives very different borough rankings depending on the measure.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
Lesson two: crossings “correlate” with casualties
Next I compared London’s roughly 5,000 small areas. The features that went up most with serious pedestrian casualties per km² were traffic signals and crossings (rank correlations of about +0.4), followed by major roads, bus stops, junctions, and pubs and bars. This was almost exactly what I had found in Athens.
That doesn’t mean crossings are dangerous. I think two things explain it:

How busy a place is. Crossings, signals, bus stops and pubs are where lots of people meet lots of traffic, so these features partly measure how busy an area is.
Cause and effect the other way round. Crossings and signals are often put in because a place had collisions.

So I also fitted a negative binomial model that takes into account how busy each area is. It asks which street features still go with more casualties after that. This is the question I couldn’t answer in my thesis with the data I had.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
Hotspots along the streets
In Athens I used planar kernel density, the usual heatmap. In a city, a cluster on one road can spill over onto a parallel street across the block. For London I measured density along the street network. I cut the streets into 50 m pieces and spread each casualty along the network for 250 m.



Where serious pedestrian injuries concentrate along London’s streets.


I also ran a Getis-Ord Gi* analysis on the small areas, to separate significant clusters from random noise. I corrected for the fact that I was testing thousands of areas at once.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
How far is emergency care?
My Athens dashboard showed the hospitals next to the collisions. For London I measured the drive time along the street network from every casualty to the nearest A&E, and to the nearest of London’s four major trauma centres, where the most seriously injured people are taken.



Free-flow drive time to the nearest major trauma centre, with serious pedestrian casualties.


These times assume no traffic and are for the journey to hospital, so they are not ambulance response times. They still show which parts of London are furthest from trauma care.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
Then and now
In 2021 I used R and ArcGIS Pro, with Esri Dashboards and StoryMaps for the visuals, and the project took months.
This time I coded with Claude, and I went from my research questions to a tested pipeline and a live dashboard much faster. The questions, the methods and what the results mean came from my research background. Claude helped me build and check everything quicker, including testing the model on made-up data with known answers before using it on the real data.
Everything uses open data and open-source Python, so anyone can run it again.

Explore the dashboard: etymo.co.uk/london-pedestrian-safety. Try the spotlight on a junction you know, or play through the years.

title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
text:
What’s next
First, I want to publish the Athens work properly, using the methods I developed here. Second, I’d like to add an AI assistant to the London data, so anyone can ask a question in plain English and get an answer worked out from the data, with its sources.

Data: Department for Transport STATS19, ONS, MHCLG (Open Government Licence); OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Police-recorded data under-reports minor pedestrian injuries, and a link between an area and casualties doesn’t show cause.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
The “15-minute city” is the idea that the things you need every day should be a short walk or bike ride from home. It is usually mapped with circles: draw 1.2 km around a GP surgery and call everything inside “15 minutes away”.
People don’t walk in circles. They walk along streets, around railway lines and rivers, and over the few places where a main road can be crossed. After my pedestrian safety project I already had London’s streets on my laptop, so I asked the question properly: how far is everything on foot, along the routes people can actually take?

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
Six everyday services
I picked six things most households need within walking distance: a GP surgery, a pharmacy, a primary school, a food shop, a park of at least 2 hectares and a rail, Tube or tram station.

Streets and paths: OpenStreetMap, including footpaths, alleys and paths through parks, not just roads a car can use. Private paths and motorways are left out.
Services: OpenStreetMap, and the Department for Education’s register for open primary schools.
People: ONS small areas, with population and the English Indices of Deprivation 2025.

I placed a “home” every 50 m along every residential and main street in London, 454,115 of them, and measured the walk from each one to the nearest of each service. One shortest-path calculation per service covers the whole city. At 4.8 km/h, the usual planning assumption, 15 minutes is 1,200 m.
58% of Londoners live within a 15-minute walk of all six. That leaves around 3.7 million people for whom at least one of them is further away. Allow 20 minutes and it rises to 79%; cut it to 10 and it falls to 23%.

Food shops, parks and primary schools are almost everywhere. The gaps are stations and GP surgeries: around a quarter of Londoners are more than 15 minutes’ walk from a station, and a fifth from a GP.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
section: Lesson one: circles flatter the city
text:
Lesson one: circles flatter the city
The straight-line column is always the higher one. Among Londoners who live within 1.2 km of a station as the crow flies, 16% are still more than a 15-minute walk away; for GPs it is 12%. Across all six services, the typical walk is 1.33 times the straight-line distance.



Share of Londoners within 15 minutes: walking along streets compared with a 1.2 km circle.


This matters beyond this map. Plenty of planning rules are drawn as circles, such as hot-food takeaway exclusion zones around schools. A circle can take in streets that are a long way round on foot and leave out ones that are close.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
section: Lesson two: it isn’t the poorest areas that miss out
text:
Lesson two: it isn’t the poorest areas that miss out
This one surprised me. The most deprived areas do better: 68% of people in England’s most deprived tenth of areas have all six within a 15-minute walk, against 37% in the least deprived tenth. Every decile in between sits between 53% and 63%, so the real outlier is the least deprived end.
In London, deprivation is concentrated in dense inner neighbourhoods where services cluster, while many of the least deprived areas are outer suburbs laid out around the car. Their residents are also more likely to have one. Closeness isn’t the same as access, though: a GP surgery ten minutes away doesn’t help if its list is full.



All six services within a 15-minute walk, by deprivation decile.


Geography explains far more. In Inner London 83% of people have all six within 15 minutes; in Outer London it is 42%. The top boroughs are Islington (99%), Hackney (96%) and Westminster (94%). At the bottom are Hillingdon (10%), Havering (20%) and Bexley (23%), all big outer boroughs where stations and GPs are spread thinly. Part of Hillingdon’s very low GP figure may be OpenStreetMap missing some surgeries, which is the first thing I’ll check against the NHS list of practices.



Boroughs ranked by the share of residents within 15 minutes of all six.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
Lesson three: 15 minutes for whom?
The 4.8 km/h figure describes a healthy adult. At 3.6 km/h, closer to an older person, a parent with a pushchair or a young child, the share within 15 minutes of all six falls from 58% to 32%. In the least deprived tenth of areas it falls to just 13%.



Within a 15-minute walk at two walking speeds.


The people who rely most on walking are the ones a 15-minute city built around an average walker reaches least.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
Try your own front door



How many of the six services are within a 15-minute walk, by small area.


The dashboard colours London by how many of the six are within reach, at your choice of pace and time. Click any spot, or type a postcode, and it walks outwards along the streets in your browser, showing how far you get in 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes and the route to the nearest of each service, with the walking and straight-line distances side by side.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
What this doesn’t tell you

Nearest isn’t always usable. A GP list can be closed to new patients, a park locked at night, a station without step-free access.
OpenStreetMap is very good in London but not perfect. A missing footpath makes a walk look longer; a missing surgery makes it look further away.
The edge of London. Services just over the boundary aren’t counted, so some homes near the edge look worse off than they are.
Homes are points along streets, not addresses. Using every address (UPRN) is the obvious next step.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
Then and now
My pedestrian project used OSMnx and Overpass to get the street network. This time the walking network is built directly from the OpenStreetMap file, footpaths and all, and the shortest-path search is a few lines of SciPy, run once per service from every location at the same time. The whole of London takes minutes on a laptop.
As before, I worked with an AI assistant, Claude. The questions and the judgement about what the numbers mean are mine. The code was tested on a made-up town where every answer can be worked out by hand, including a private shortcut it must ignore, before I trusted it with London.

title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
text:
What’s next
Three things. Using address points (UPRNs) instead of street points for homes. Turning the takeaway exclusion zones in my Takeaways Near Schools tool into real walking distances. And running the same code on other cities, since nothing in it is specific to London.

Data: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL); Department for Education, ONS and MHCLG (Open Government Licence). Walking times assume a constant pace and ignore waiting at crossings, hills and steps, so real walks are a little longer.

title: About
text:
I’m Eriola Trungu Impersimi, a Government Operational Researcher and geospatial analyst. I’ve worked with quantitative, geospatial and statistical methods for more than 15 years, in government, academia and the private sector.
I like taking messy data and making it clear, explaining uncertainty, and building tools that help people make decisions. Lately I’ve been trying out how AI can make spatial analysis faster and easier for more people, while keeping it rigorous.
What I write about here

Spatial analysis and mapping, from road safety to nature-based solutions
Statistics and modelling for decisions, including forecasting and uncertainty
Data quality and reproducible pipelines
Working with AI as an analyst: what it speeds up, and what still needs judgement

I hold an MSc in Geoinformatics from the National Technical University of Athens, where my thesis analysed pedestrian collisions and the built environment in Athens.
Why etymo? It comes from the Greek etymon (ἔτυμον), the true meaning of something. That’s what I look for in data. And ET is me.
